quote: But as Davidson once observed, if you believe that “beavers” live in deserts, are pure white in color, and weigh 300 pounds when adult, then you do not have any beliefs about beavers, true or false.
content: The footnote cites a popular obituary by Rorty rather than Davidson, and the principle is contested. On the causal theory of reference developed by Kripke (Naming and Necessity, 1980; book, no DOI) and Putnam (1973), a word can refer to its object even when nearly everything the speaker believes about it is false, provided the right causal-historical chain links them. Kripke's Gödel/Schmidt case is the standard example. If reference works that way, a person can be talking about morality while knowing almost nothing true about it, which is exactly the position the essay calls incoherent.

quote: There are no-free-lunch theorems in computer science—in a maxentropy universe, no plan is better on average than any other.
content: That's not what the no-free-lunch theorems say. Wolpert & Macready (1997) show that when performance is averaged uniformly over all possible objective functions, all search algorithms do equally well. "Maxentropy universe" is the essay's gloss, and the theorems concern optimization, not knowledge of morality or the meaning of words. Their usual moral is that any algorithm that succeeds must exploit structure in the problems it faces, which says nothing about whether morality has such structure.

quote: could be presented with the coherence and uniqueness proofs underlying Bayesian probability, and that might change their definition of evidence
content: The uniqueness claim overstates the proofs. Cox's theorem, the usual "uniqueness proof," fails under its stated assumptions (Halpern 1999). Dutch-book arguments establish coherence only given further assumptions about betting and value. And there are coherent alternatives the proofs don't exclude: imprecise probabilities, ranking functions, Dempster–Shafer belief. Bayesian confirmation theory also has well-known problems of its own, such as the problem of old evidence (Glymour, Theory and Evidence, 1980; book, no DOI). A Popperian presented with these proofs wouldn't be facing a knockdown argument.

quote: Why not accept that, ceteris paribus, joy is preferable to sorrow?
content: The essay's argument licenses at most the minimal commitments needed for "right" to mean something, namely that morality is what you argue about when you argue about morality. The next step slips in substantive moral content ("joy is preferable to sorrow") as though it were part of the word's meaning. By the same route a believer can "bake in" that God's commands are right, and an ascetic that sorrow ennobles. Commitments that fix a word's meaning and substantive moral commitments have to be kept apart. Here the essay's reasonable claim about the first is used to smuggle in the second.

quote: I don’t argue by definitions, of course.
content: The essay argues by definition throughout. Its central claim is that words like "right" have content "baked into" their very meaning, and that someone who claims to know nothing about morality "will have problems with the meaning of your words." That is an argument about definitions. The disclaimer lets the reader accept the argument while believing it is not the kind the sequence warns against ("Arguing 'By Definition'").
